On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya held the power: he kicked open the locked door sword in hand and gave Sitaram orders, while Sitaram only obeyed, refused to take up arms against the Yubaraj who had twice saved his life, and begged to be disarmed and bound head to foot so he could face the Maharaj's wrath. On the night of Udayaditya's escape the roles invert: Sitaram becomes the leader and rescuer—he first hurries Basanta Ray away, then raises the cry of fire, opens the prison door, and nearly carries Udayaditya out—while Udayaditya is passive and dependent, asking "Why?" and then helplessly, "What should I do? Where should I go?"

Pratapaditya's initial plan was to send two Pathan men to kill Basanta Ray when he sheltered at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore, but it failed when the Pathan (Khan Saheb) could not bring himself to commit the murder and instead fled to Udayaditya, feigning coercion. The method that finally succeeded was a written order signed by Pratapaditya himself, carried out by Muktiyar Khan at Raigarh: while Basanta Ray was finishing his evening prayers, Muktiyar had his man Abdul come in with a drawn sword, and Basanta Ray was executed by the sword.

In the Mahishi's room, disguised as a middle-aged woman — Rammohan seized his hands, tore off his head cloth to reveal Ramai Thakur, swung him in the air, then tied him in a shawl and carried him off; and in the king's chamber, undisguised as himself, the jester Ramai Bhand — Rammohan grabbed him by the scruff of the neck and threw him out of the room.

The Rajmahishi secretly obtained a "medicine" from the widow Mangala (actually Rukmini), who spent five days preparing a poison with mantras; Surma took this poison and died—so her actual departure was death by poison, not exile.

Rammohan returns to Chandradwip alone, and King Ramchandra Ray takes Vibha's refusal as a mortal insult to his honor and dynasty; in wounded pride and thirst for revenge, he resolves to take another wife and finalizes the wedding plans. Thus, when Vibha finally agrees to go, it is too late—the Maharaj is already getting married, and she learns that in her own husband's kingdom there is no place for her, her hopes shattered like a mirage.

Rukmini obtains the ring during a stormy night visit, playing on Udayaditya's guilt and grief over Surma until he pulls it from his finger and throws it to her. The ring bears the Yubaraj's name engraved as a seal. Sitaram and Bhagavat exploit this: they forge a petition in Udayaditya's name, as if he were accusing Pratapaditya of treason before the Emperor to seize the kingdom for himself, and stamp it with the seal from the ring, which makes the forgery credible. Bhagavat delivers it to Pratapaditya, claiming a servant of Udayaditya was caught carrying it toward Delhi and fled, leaving it behind. Enraged by the sealed petition, Pratapaditya uses it as evidence of treason to order Udayaditya imprisoned — though he admits he doesn't truly believe the Yubaraj guilty, reasoning there is no harm in keeping him locked away under guard regardless.

The escape ruined the guards who had failed to stop it: Sitaram, whom Udayaditya disarmed and bound that night, and Bhagavat were dismissed from the palace and left destitute. Feeling responsible, Udayaditya set them a monthly stipend; Pratapaditya furiously forbade it, yet the aid still flowed secretly through Surma's maid. When word of the secret stipends reached Pratapaditya's ears, he read them as defiance of his express command, and rather than confront Udayaditya directly he ordered Surma to her paternal home—knowing, as the Mahishi warned, that Uday could not survive her exile, so the decree struck him through her.

The song is a lament of total desolation — the singer is the sole survivor, everything and everyone he loved has vanished, and even singing itself has lost its joy. It expresses the collapse of his world into emptiness and loneliness.

First context: in Raigarh, Basanta Ray hums it alone on the veranda at sunset, a private, spontaneous outpouring to himself — grieving his lost companion (the sitar) and the absence of those he longed to embrace, with no one to hear him.

Second context: in Jessore, after standing silently before the dark, empty, silent room of Surma, he slowly begins to sing it while holding Vibha's hand — the same lament now shared with the last broken remnant of his family, transforming solitary grief into communal mourning over the deserted household.

Rukmini's failure to stop the escape drives her straight to Pratapaditya's court, where she reveals the flight, names Sitaram and Basanta Ray as co-conspirators, and demands men to hunt the fugitives down. Pratapaditya sends her out with soldiers, and her party tracks Udayaditya to Raigarh, where she remains; her intelligence thus brings the king's forces to the old king's doorstep. That same night she spots Udayaditya alone in the field and cries out his location, letting the soldiers surround and seize him. With Udayaditya captured, Muktiyar Khan can execute the secret death sentence Pratapaditya has issued against Basanta Ray—an order Udayaditya believes was meant to fall on the old king if the escapee could not be found—and so Basanta Ray is beheaded as his nephew is led away prisoner.

Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra with deliberate calm and minimal ceremony—no fanfare or lit path, a late and modest welcome party, and a composed, businesslike meeting that ends by dismissing him to the inner quarters—conveying superiority through restraint, which Ramchandra himself recognizes. In contrast, Ramchandra later compensates for that wounded pride with loud, relentless disparagement in his own court: daily ritualized ridicule of Pratapaditya's humble lineage, jokes about his father's plea for anointment, punishment of anyone who merely compares them, and a steady stream of verbal arrows from his courtiers. Where Pratapaditya asserts dominance through quiet composure, Ramchandra asserts it through noisy mockery and manufactured slights—revealing that his bluster springs from insecurity rather than genuine supremacy.

Rukmini, the elder widow from Raigarh who had lured Udayaditya in his youth, reappears under the name Mangala, living on the outskirts of Jessore. She befriends the palace servants to track every scrap of news, performs rites for the deaths of Pratapaditya and Surma, and dreams of ruling the Yubaraj's heart and the kingdom once he ascends the throne. When the Rajmahishi, desperate to win her son back from Surma before driving her out, sends for a widow versed in tantra and medicine, Mangala seizes the chance: she spends five days grinding roots and chanting mantras to prepare a poison that will make the prince feel no pity, and Surma dies after taking it. Later, on a stormy night, she slips into Udayaditya's darkened bedchamber while he sits with a sleeping girl, lets him believe at first that Surma has returned, then reveals herself, reproaches him for ruining her, seats herself on Surma's bed, and extorts the ring from his finger before leaving him collapsed in grief—thus turning his old sin into present tragedy.

Udayaditya's early wish to have never been born crown prince—feeling unfit, tested, and neglected by his father—reaches its fulfillment when he is brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner and declares himself unworthy of the kingdom, asking only for release from the throne. He swears an oath at Ma-Kali's feet, in front of his father, that he will never accept even an iota of Jessore's kingdom, never sit on its throne or touch its royal scepter, invoking the sin of his grand-uncle's murder as the penalty should he break it; he names Samaraditya as heir and asks only for money to build a guest house and temple in his grand-uncle's name in Kashi, then prepares to leave as an ascetic. The wish he voiced to Surma in Chapter 1—"I wish I had not been born... the sole heir"—is thus formally enacted: he renounces the throne, the scepter, and the palace, keeping only the duty of seeing Vibha married before his exile.

Nayanchand, charged with delivering Ramchandra Ray's letter to Pratapaditya, was too afraid of what the king might do and instead gave it to the Mahishi. She hid the letter, showing it only to Basanta Ray, who—stunned by its true contents (that Ramchandra had renounced Vibha and ordered her not be sent to Chandradwip)—advised her to keep it secret and to announce in the household that Ramchandra had written requesting Vibha be sent to her in-laws' house. The Mahishi did so, telling Vibha and the household this inverted version, which filled Vibha with joy and the belief that her husband had forgiven and longed for her.

Pratapaditya had the canal beside the palace blocked with large sal-wood logs and posted guards to seal the inner quarters, but the trap collapsed on execution: Rammohan and his followers simply hauled Ramchandra's boat up and over the logs. The guards could only throw stones that never reached the boat—they had swords but no guns, and the one flintlock they found had no gunpowder or bullets. The pursuit boat arrived far too late because the man sent to fetch it stopped to smoke at Harimudi's shop and woke Ramashankar to demand repayment of a debt, and the subsequent scolding consumed even more time, leaving no chance of catching the boat.

The sitar mirrors Basanta Ray's grief: in his farewell he plays it furiously, but tears blur his eyes and choke his throat until he must stop, and he leaves it behind vowing never to play again. By the time news of Udayaditya's imprisonment reaches him, his "eternal companion" is gone, and he explains that the sitar is there but its strings are broken and can no longer be tuned—an emblem of his own shattered, untunable spirit. Yet when Khan Saheb sings, he leaps up to join in, showing the music still lives in him even as the sitar itself is silenced, so the broken instrument figures a despair that is deep but not total.

Earlier, Udayaditya freely involved himself in his subjects' affairs, defied Pratapaditya's wishes, and confronted oppression without weighing danger—he would rush to stop an official beating a subject and shield the victim, and he treated danger as a trifle. After Surma's death, a blind fear of Pratapaditya paralyzes him: he orders the horse for the Chhra raid then sends it away, runs from the beaten subject, and never sends money to Bhagavat and Sitaram, hesitating in every task as if his fate rested in Pratapaditya's fist.

Sitaram engineers Udayaditya's escape from prison: in the evening he raises the alarm that the prison is on fire, rushes to Udayaditya's cell, grabs him and carries him out into the open field, then takes him away to safety ("Come, come with me!") — freeing him from the imprisonment that the forged petition he conspired with Bhagavat to create had brought about.

On the first occasion, he rescues Ramchandra Ray from Jessore palace: after Udayaditya collects thick sheets, Rammohan twists and ties them into a huge rope anchored to a pillar on the roof, ties the king to his back, and climbs down the seventy cubits to the canal, gripping the rope with his teeth at the end to lower Ramchandra by hand into the sixty-four-oared boat before jumping down himself, then hauls the boat over the blocking sal logs and escapes.

On the second occasion, he rescues Vibha: when the king fails to recognize his Mahishi and she faints from shame, Rammohan hurls the mocking jester Ramai Bhand out of the room, declares he is leaving the king's service forever, lifts the unconscious Vibha, carries her out through the palace gate, places her in a waiting palanquin, and returns with her to the boat to take her to Kashi.

In Jessore, Vibha is a royally adorned princess: the Mahishi dresses her with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and a carefully styled coiffure—she is flushed with shy, suppressed joy, resplendent and veiled. In Chandradwip, she deliberately strips all this away: she dresses as a common woman, refuses a palanquin, insists on going "like a beggar-woman" on foot, her veil falls in the crowd, she slips into the palace unrecognized like a maidservant, and falls at the king's feet to give away her everything. The shift runs from ornate display and concealed delight to utter plainness and public surrender—adornment exchanged for humiliation, the blushing bride for the prostrate supplicant.

In the bedchamber, the window is a site of absence and haunting grief. Surma used to sit by that window, so Udayaditya sits there and leaves her place empty; the unchanged view—same moonlight, same garden, same breeze—only underscores that she will not come, and it is there that he half-expects to hear her voice. The window frames loss: the world outside continues exactly as before, indifferent to his sorrow, and the window becomes a memorial to the dead, binding him to the past.

In the prison cell, the window's meaning inverts into a symbol of freedom and hope. Though it is tiny—a sliver of sky, a bamboo grove, a temple—it is through it that he sees birds fly and imagines his cage breaking, himself swimming in that endless sky. He keeps his face near the window rather than on the bed, because away from it he sees only darkness and forgets liberation; in that small patch of space he feels naturally free, beyond any king's power. Where the broad bedchamber window brought only sorrow, the narrow prison window opens toward the future—the smaller the opening, the larger the promise of deliverance.

It begins as a transactional flirtation: Sitaram, a penniless dandy, borrows from Rukmini the moneylender, dodges repayment, and courts her with pet names and jesting while the two confer in secret. The turn comes with the Yubaraj's imprisonment: Sitaram curses her to her face, nearly strikes her, and threatens to burn her house and smear her face with lime and soot, while she declares the Yubaraj is *hers* alone—affection has become a contest of ownership over him. The encounter turns life-threatening when Sitaram, having engineered the Yubaraj's escape and faked death, hears Rukmini is dead and breaks into her cottage to rob her, only to find her alive, drenched and spectral in the lamplight; she threatens to consecrate herself with ash from his and the Yubaraj's pyres, hunts him with a curved blade, and he flees the city that night. His greed at the robbery, her survival, and her knowledge of the escape make it lethal, and she carries the feud to the king, exposing Sitaram's role and vowing to track the fugitives down.

Sitaram begins with the fire as a diversion: he alerts Udayaditya that the prison is on fire and nearly carries him out, exploiting the fact that the guards at his door—who kept watch only out of custom, since Udayaditya never seemed to desire escape—were the first to flee. What starts as a simple distraction is then deliberately deepened by sabotage: Sitaram's men, mixed among the firefighters, pour water where there is no fire, fetch water and never return, and break their pots, so the blaze cannot be contained. The crucial escalation comes after Udayaditya is safely away—they set fire to the now-empty cell itself, burning its windows, doors, beams and fences in a place where everyone assumes a fire is impossible, so no one pays attention. Sitaram then converts chaos into evidence: having earlier taken the Yubaraj's sword, he throws it, along with bones and a skull, into the burning room, while his accomplices shout that Udayaditya was heard screaming and that the roof has collapsed with no response. Thus the distraction becomes a staged death: Sitaram plants physical proof, supplies witnesses, and spreads the rumor that the Yubaraj died in the flames, planning to remain untroubled. He also intercepts Udayaditya's letters, destroying all but those for the Mahishi and Vibha, and flees the city. The cover-up nearly holds until Rukmini bursts into court to name him as the arsonist, and fishermen and travelers confirm the escape, exposing the whole scheme.

Ramchandra Ray feels no gratitude at all. In his court he joins the daily jesting at Pratapaditya's expense, bringing up Udayaditya's name and laughing at him, as if Udayaditya's only crime is being Pratapaditya's son—the fact that Udayaditya ignored his own danger to save the king's life "went up in smoke." Being fickle and small-minded, he assumes saving him was bound to happen (not to do so would have been wrong) and that everyone would unite to save him in peril, and he believes Udayaditya's real motive was his own sister Vibha rather than the king's life. Even had gratitude stirred, he would still have joined the mockery: with Ramai Bhand leading the jeers, he lacks the nerve to silence the court or refrain, thinking only of what everyone else would think. Notably, that very night he also developed a brief infatuation with the crying Vibha, which reinforced his suspicion that Udayaditya acted for his sister's sake.

Pratapaditya treats the Emperor of Delhi as an empty threat — "not my God," someone whose anger only makes others tremble — and even forbids the minister from speaking his name. Yet the Emperor's authority is precisely what the conspirators weaponize: Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition accusing Pratapaditya of treason, written as if the Yubaraj (Udayaditya) were complaining against his own father to the Emperor in order to seize the kingdom, and stamp it with the Yubaraj's seal from the ring Rukmini had brought. Instead of sending it to Delhi, Bhagavat intercepts it (or pretends to), telling Pratapaditya that a servant of Udayaditya was carrying it to the Emperor and fled, leaving the petition behind. The fabricated "complaint to the Emperor" thus converts the remote political specter Pratapaditya scorned into direct, seemingly documentary proof of his son's treason — the very accusation Pratapaditya had feared and half-suspected Udayaditya of — and it is this forged petition that delivers the son into his father's power, while also restoring Bhagavat to his post at the palace.

Vibha's hair is braided only by Surma, whose touch is so tied to her that when Vibha secretly has Surma style it to her own taste, the Mahishi detects the change and undoes it. After Surma's disappearance, Vibha cannot bring herself to braid her hair at all: at braiding time she sits quietly waiting as if Surma will come, but evening falls and her hair remains unbraided—the unperformed ritual itself becoming the marker of loss. Later, Rammohan observes that her hair is unkempt, making the neglected coiffure a visible emblem of her grief and abandonment. Thus a well-groomed braid signals Surma's living presence and care, while the unbraided, unkempt hair testifies to her absence and Vibha's desolation.
